## Data Acquisition

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Click here to show/hide the Code"
#' Acquire Netflix What We Watched Reports
#' 
#' This function will acquire and standardize all data for MP#01
#' from Netflix. Because Netflix hosts the data files behind a CDN, we
#' are accessing the release pages and automatically extracting links to the
#' relevant files (with CDN hash). 
#' 
#' After import, files are stacked vertically and some basic cleaning is
#' performed. 
#' Acquire Netflix What We Watched Reports
#' 
#' This function will acquire and standardize all data for MP#01
#' from Netflix. Because Netflix hosts the data files behind a CDN, we
#' are accessing the release pages and automatically extracting links to the
#' relevant files (with CDN hash). 
#' 
#' After import, files are stacked vertically and some basic cleaning is
#' performed. 
load_netflix_data <- function(){
  # Note to students: Make sure you have installed the tidyverse and fs packages
  #                   before beginning this assignment. If you aren't sure,
  #                   simply run `library(tidyverse)` at your R Console and, if
  #                   you don't see an error message, `tidyverse` has been 
  #                   installed. (Same for `fs`) If you still need to install
  #                   either package, use the `install.packages` function as 
  #                   demonstrated in class.

  
  data_dir <- path("data", "mp01")
  
  if(!dir_exists(data_dir)){
    dir_create(data_dir, showWarnings=FALSE, recurse=TRUE)
  }
  
  NETFLIX_URLS <- list(
    `2023H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-a-netflix-engagement-report",
    `2023H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2023",
    `2024H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2024",
    `2024H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2024",
    `2025H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2025",
    `2025H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2025",
    `2026H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2026"
  )
  
  download_if_needed <- function(url, local){
    if(!file_exists(local)){
      download.file(url, local, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb")
    }

    return(local)
  }
  
  NETFLIX_URLS |> 
    map(read_html) |> 
    map(html_element, xpath = "//a[contains(@href, '.xlsx')]") |> 
    map_chr(html_attr, "href") |> 
    enframe("period", "url") |> 
    mutate(path = path(data_dir, paste0(period, ".xlsx")), 
           path = map2(url, path, download_if_needed), 
           data = map(path, read_excel, skip=3, na="*"), 
           data = map(data, \(x) x |> mutate(`Release Date` = as.Date(`Release Date`)))) |>
    unnest(data) |> 
    select(-url, -path) |> 
    mutate(year=str_sub(period, 1, 4), 
           half=str_sub(period, start=6), 
           period_start = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 1, 7), 1), 
           period_end = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 6, 12), if_else(half==1, 30, 31))) |> 
    filter(!is.na(`Hours Viewed`)) |> 
    mutate(live_event = !is.na(Runtime) & str_detect(Runtime, "\\d+:\\d+\\*"), 
           clean_time = str_remove(Runtime, fixed("*")),
           Runtime = 60 * hour(hm(clean_time)) + minute(hm(clean_time))) |>
    select(-clean_time) |>
    mutate(Runtime = coalesce(Runtime, mean(Runtime, na.rm=TRUE)), 
           .by=Title, 
           Title = stringi::stri_trans_general(Title, "Latin-ASCII"),
           Title = str_remove(Title, " // .*"), 
           Title = str_remove(Title, "[^[:ascii:]].*"), 
           Title = str_trim(Title)) |>
    filter_out(Title == "") |>
    select(year, 
           period, 
           period_start, 
           period_end, 
           Title, 
           -half, 
           Runtime, 
           Views, 
           `Hours Viewed`, 
           `Release Date`,
           `Available Globally?`, 
           live_event) |>
    rename_with(clean_column_name)
}

# Function for renaming the columns by following the 4 rules listed on the web.
clean_column_name <- function(column_name){
  column_name <- column_name |>
    # All lower-case
    tolower() |>
    # If multi-word, separated by underscores (_) not spaces
    gsub(" ", "_", x = _) |>
    # Only numbers and simple letters, no punctuation or accents
    gsub("[^a-z0-9_]", "", x = _) |>
    # Starting with a letter
    gsub("^[^a-z]", "", x = _)
  
  return(column_name)
}

NETFLIX_DATA <- load_netflix_data()
ORIGINAL_NETFLIX_DATA <- NETFLIX_DATA #  to store the original Netflix data

```

## Data Cleaning and Preparation

### Fix Columns Title

Renaming the columns is done inside the `clean_column_name()` function and satisfied these four rules:

- All lower-case: `tolower()`
- If multi-word, separated by underscores (_) not spaces: `gsub(" ", "_", x = _)`
- Only numbers and simple letters, no punctuation or accents: `gsub("[^a-z0-9_]", "", x = _)`
- Starting with a letter: `gsub("^[^a-z]", "", x = _)`

Result:
```{r}
NETFLIX_DATA |> names()
```

### Fix Columns Type

Before we fix the columns type of the data frame, it is important to check how `R` thinks our data is. By using `glimpse()` function, we can determine object types from the data frame.

```{r}
NETFLIX_DATA |> glimpse()
```

The result shows that column `$year` has `<chr>` datatype which we need to convert it to `<int>` data type. Not only that, column `$available_globally` has `<chr>` datatype whereas it has "Yes" or "No" values. It would be wiser if we convert those values to logical values either `TRUE` or `FALSE`.

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
#| code-summary: "Click here to show/hide the Code"
NETFLIX_DATA <-  NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(
    year = as.integer(year),
    available_globally = available_globally == "Yes"    
  )
```

### Analysis

There are 2 problems in this dataset:

1. Number of missing value between column `$runtime` and column `$views` shows difference, whereas column `$views` is calculated by dividing `$hours_viewed` by `$runtime`.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Click here to show/hide the Code"
NETFLIX_DATA <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(
    views = if_else(
      !is.na(runtime) & runtime > 0, 
      round(hours_viewed * 60 / runtime), 
      NA_real_
    )
  )

NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summary()
```

2. Two rows have missing value in column `$available_globally`. We have 2 options, drop it or fill the missing value with TRUE or FALSE. The problem is: which option should we choose?.

By logic, dropping 2 of 61,892 rows will not hurt the analysis result. But, let's take a look which rows have the missing value.

```{r}
NETFLIX_DATA |> filter(is.na(available_globally))
```

They have same title "Other Shows" which I assume it's a combination of many shows. Therefore, drop the rows is the best option we can take.

```{r}
NETFLIX_DATA <- NETFLIX_DATA |> filter_out(is.na(available_globally))
```

## Exploratory Questions

### Inline Values

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Click here to show/hide the Code"

# 1 and 2
movies_date_range <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarize(
    started = min(period_start, na.rm = TRUE), 
    ended = max(period_end, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_titles = n_distinct(title)
  )

# 3
bridgerton_hours_watched <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, regex("Bridgerton", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  summarize(total_hours_watched = sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(total_hours_watched)

bridgerton_start_date <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, regex("Bridgerton", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  summarize(start_date = 
    max(
      min(period_start, na.rm = TRUE), 
      min(release_date, na.rm = TRUE)
    )
  ) |>
  pull(start_date)

# 4
stranger_things_rows <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(
    str_detect(title, regex("Stranger Things", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    !str_detect(title, ":")) |>
  summarize(
    total_hours_watched = sum(hours_viewed),
    start_date = max(
      min(period_start, na.rm = TRUE), 
      min(release_date, na.rm = TRUE))
  )

strangers_hours <- stranger_things_rows$total_hours_watched
strangers_start_date <- stranger_things_rows$start_date

# 5
n_2026H1_movies <- NETFLIX_DATA |> 
  filter(period == "2026H1") |>
  summarize(n_movies = n()) |> pull(n_movies)

top_movies <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(period == "2026H1") |>
  mutate(
    overall_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  slice_max(hours_viewed, n=round(0.2 * n_2026H1_movies), with_ties = FALSE) |> # to get 20% of most watched movie
  mutate(
    top_20percent_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  slice_max(hours_viewed, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  summarize(
    top_10_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    top_20percent_hours = first(top_20percent_hours),
    overall_hours = first(overall_hours),
    top_10_percentage  = percent((top_10_hours / overall_hours), accuracy = 0.01), 
    top_20percent_percentage  = percent((top_20percent_hours / overall_hours), accuracy = 0.01), 
  )

top_10_hours <- top_movies$top_10_hours
top_20percent_hours <- top_movies$top_20percent_hours
overall_hours <- top_movies$overall_hours
top_10_percentage <- top_movies$top_10_percentage
top_20percent_percentage <- top_movies$top_20percent_percentage

# 6
by_title <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  distinct(title, available_globally) |>
  summarize(
    n_global = sum(available_globally),
    n_all = n(),
    n_percentage = round((n_global / n_all * 100), digits = 2)
  )

by_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarize(
    hours_global = sum(if_else(available_globally, hours_viewed, 0), na.rm=TRUE), 
    hours_all = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm=TRUE),
    hours_percentage = round((hours_global / hours_all * 100), digits = 2)
  )
```

1. What date range is covered by this data set?\
The dataset covers movies report start from `r format(movies_date_range$started, "%B %d, %Y")` through `r format(movies_date_range$ended, "%B %d, %Y")`.

2. How many different shows and movies are covered in this data set?\
There are `r comma(movies_date_range$n_titles)` total different titles across the dataset.

3. How many total hours have been spent watching shows from the Bridgerton universe?\
The Bridgerton universe accumulated total `r comma(bridgerton_hours_watched)` hours viewed since `r format(bridgerton_start_date, "%B, %Y")`.

4. How many total hours have been spent watching the five seasons of Stranger Things? (Only the real Stranger Things shows)\
The Stranger Things shows (the main 5 seasons of Stranger Things) accumulated total `r comma(strangers_hours)` hours viewed since `r format(strangers_start_date, "%B, %Y")`.

5. What percentage of total watch time was spent on the Top 10 titles of 2026H1?\
The top 10 titles (by total watch time) in 2026 first half period has total `r comma(top_10_hours)` hours watched which makes the top 10 titles shows or movies covered total `{r} top_10_percentage` of total watch time in 2026 first half period.\
  This questions leads to the **Pareto principle** or **80/20 rule**, is the idea that a small share of things (~20%) can be account for a large share (~80%) of the result. Using the NETFLIX watched hours data, top 20% most-watched shows or movies in 2026 first half accumulates total `r comma(top_20percent_hours)` hours. This number covers total `{r} top_20percent_percentage` of total watched hours in the first half of 2026.

6. What fraction of Netflix’s catalog is globally available? (Answer this both by title and weighted by hours viewed)\
**By title**, there are total `r comma(by_title$n_global)` different shows or movies that globally available of `r comma(by_title$n_all)` total shows or movies. The fraction is $\frac{`{r} comma(by_title$n_global)`}{`{r} comma(by_title$n_all)`} \approx `{r} by_title$n_percentage`\%$\
  **By total hours viewed**, there is total `r comma(by_hours$hours_global)` watching hours from the shows or movies that are globally available of `r comma(by_hours$hours_all)` total hours across all shows or movies. The fraction is $\frac{`{r} comma(by_hours$hours_global)`}{`{r} comma(by_hours$hours_all)`} \approx `{r} by_hours$hours_percentage`\%$


### Table Answer

1. What was the top title (by total hours viewed) in each period and what fraction of total viewership did it capture?\

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Click here to show/hide the Code"
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  select(period, title, hours_viewed) |>
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(
    total_hours = sum(hours_viewed),
    percentage = percent((hours_viewed / total_hours), accuracy = 0.01)
  ) |>
  slice_max(hours_viewed, n = 1) |>
  select(-total_hours) |>
  ungroup() |>
  gt() |> 
  tab_header(title=md("**Top NETFLIX Title Every Period**")) |>
  cols_label(
    period = md("Period"), 
    title = md("Top Title"), 
    hours_viewed = md("Hours Viewed"),
    percentage = md("Share of Total Hours Viewed")         
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = hours_viewed,
    decimals = 0,
    use_seps = TRUE
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(
    columns = percentage,
    decimals = 2
  ) |>
  opt_row_striping()
```

2. How has Netflix’s catalog changed in size over the periods for which we have questions? You should consider both the number of titles and the total runtime of content.\

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Click here to show/hide the Code"

NETFLIX_DATA |>
  select(period, title, runtime) |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarize(
    n_title = n(),
    total_runtime = sum(runtime, na.rm = TRUE)/60
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(title_change = n_title / lag(n_title) - 1) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = md("**Netflix Catalog Size Over The Period**")) |>
  cols_label(
    period = "Period",
    n_title = "Number of Titles",
    total_runtime = md("Total Known Runtime (*hours*)"),
    title_change = "Title Change"
  ) |>
  cols_move_to_end(total_runtime) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(n_title, total_runtime),
    decimals = 0,
    use_seps = TRUE
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(
    title_change, decimals = 2
  ) |>
  opt_row_striping()

```

3. Which titles have had the most consistently high viewership across all periods? These shows are likely to be ‘staples’ that viewers fall back on as ‘comfort food’.\
```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Click here to show/hide the Code"

staples <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(title) |>
  summarize(
    periods = n_distinct(period),
    mean_hours = mean(hours_viewed),
    min_hours = min(hours_viewed),
    sd_hours = sd(hours_viewed)
  ) |> ungroup() |>
  # Take top 1% average watched hours
  filter(periods > 4, mean_hours > quantile(mean_hours, probs = 0.99, na.rm=TRUE)) |>
  mutate(
    z_min_hours_score = abs(min_hours - mean_hours)/sd_hours,
    cv = sd_hours / mean_hours
  ) |>
  filter(cv <= 0.4, z_min_hours_score <= 1.5) |>
  arrange(desc(min_hours)) |>
  select(-z_min_hours_score)

staples |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = md("**Consistent Viewing Staples**"),
             subtitle = "Observed in minimum five periods; CV ≤ 40%; Z-score ≤ 1.5; Ranked by minimum hours") |>
  cols_label(
    title = "Title",
    periods = "Periods",
    mean_hours = "Average Hours Viewed",
    min_hours = "Minimum Hours Viewed",
    sd_hours = "SD Hours Viewed",
    cv = "Coefficient of Variation (CV)"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(mean_hours, min_hours, sd_hours),
    decimals = 0,
    use_seps = TRUE
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(
    cv, decimals = 2
  ) |>
  opt_row_striping()
  
```
  I use **Coefficient of Variation (CV)** to measure variability relative to mean. I limited the CV to 40% or less because the higher CV shows the data has bigger spread of data (standard deviation) which shows the inconsistency watched hours over the period.


4. Within each period, what fraction of time was spent on ‘shows’ vs movies?\
```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Click here to show/hide the Code"
classified <- NETFLIX_DATA |> 
  mutate(
    content_type = case_when(
      live_event ~ "Live Event",
      str_detect(title, regex("season|series", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "TV Show",
      runtime > 240 ~ "TV Show",
      TRUE ~ "Movie"
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarize(
    total_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    live_frac = sum(ifelse(content_type == "Live Event", hours_viewed, 0), na.rm = TRUE)/total_hours,
    show_frac = sum(ifelse(content_type == "TV Show", hours_viewed, 0), na.rm = TRUE)/total_hours,
    movie_frac = sum(ifelse(content_type == "Movie", hours_viewed, 0), na.rm = TRUE)/total_hours
  )

classified |> 
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = md("**Live vs TV Show vs Movie Watched Hours Percentage**")) |>
  cols_move_to_end(total_hours) |>
  cols_label(
    period = "Period",
    total_hours = "Total Watched Hours",
    live_frac = "Live Event(%)",
    show_frac = "TV Show(%)",
    movie_frac = "Movie(%)"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = total_hours,
    decimals = 0,
    use_seps = TRUE
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(
    c(live_frac, show_frac, movie_frac), decimals = 2
  ) |>
  opt_row_striping()

```
  TV Shows dominated total watched hours across all Netflix's content. The result shows that starting 2023H2, TV Show generated more than 97% of total watching hours.

5. How does the performance of live events compare to pre-taped content? Does the average live event draw more viewership than an average piece of pre-taped content? How about a ‘top tier’ live event vs ‘top tier’ pre-taped content?\


```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Click here to show/hide the Code"
format_content_rows <-NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(format_content = ifelse(live_event, "Live Event", "Pre-Taped")) |>
  group_by(period, format_content) |>
  mutate(
    avg_hours = mean(hours_viewed, na.rm=TRUE),
    top_tier_bar = quantile(avg_hours, probs = 0.99, na.rm=TRUE),
    is_toptier = ifelse(hours_viewed >= top_tier_bar, TRUE, FALSE),
    toptier_viewed_hour = ifelse(is_toptier, hours_viewed, NA_real_),
    nontoptier_viewed_hour = ifelse(!is_toptier, hours_viewed, NA_real_)
  ) |>
  summarize(
    avg_hours_viewed = mean(hours_viewed, na.rm=TRUE),
    avg_top_tier = mean(toptier_viewed_hour, na.rm=TRUE),
    avg_nontop_tier = mean(nontoptier_viewed_hour, na.rm=TRUE),
    .groups = "drop_last"
  )

format_content_rows |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = md("**Live vs Pre-Taped Content Comparison Table**"),
             subtitle = md("Average viewed hours for each format content")) |>
  cols_move_to_end(avg_hours_viewed) |>
  cols_label(
    format_content = "Format Content",
    avg_hours_viewed = "All",
    avg_top_tier = "Top Tier",
    avg_nontop_tier = "Common"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(avg_hours_viewed,avg_top_tier,avg_nontop_tier),
    decimals = 0,
    use_seps = TRUE
  ) |>
  opt_row_striping()
```
  In almost all periods, the pre-taped content dominated the live event content in Netflix. The only period when top-tier live event contents overcome the top-tier pre-taped contents average watched hours is in 2025H2 period.\
  Let's check what are the titles for the top-tier live event contents in 2025H2 period.
```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Click here to show/hide the Code"
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(
    live_event,
    period == "2024H2"
  ) |>
  select(period, title, hours_viewed)
```


## Corporate Strategy Memo

**TO: Netflix Leadership Team**\
**Subject: Content Strategy for 2027 and Beyond**\


**Summary**\
As we head into 2027, staying as number 1 in streaming means we can't just guess what people want to watch and hoping people will choose Netflix over other streaming platform. We have take a look at the actual number, not just by what we believe. Based on the 2023 to first half of 2026 viewing hours data across the titles in Netflix, here's my take on how Netflix should tweak its original content game plan.\

**1. Globally available vs. regionally licensed content**\
I found out that effective as of 2023 to first half of 2026, there are total `r comma(by_title$n_global)` different contents that globally available of `r comma(by_title$n_all)` total contents. The percentage is just `{r} percent(by_title$n_percentage, accuracy = 2)`. From this small percentage, all contents that is globally available capable to accumulate total `{r} percent(by_hours$hours_percentage, accuracy = 2)`.\
By this data, globally available contents dominated more than half of total viewed with only less than quarter number of titles across all titles. It showed that the contents that are available globally could make people to keep watching Netflix for long-term. \
**Recommendation**: Keep the regionally licensed contents for short-term engagement buffer, but double down on global IP rights to secure long-term value.\

**2. TV Shows vs. Movies**\
TV Shows drive more than 97% of total watching hours for 3 years, starting from H2 2023 through H1 2026. TV shows are doing all the heavy lifting, no doubt, it's because of the long-runtime TV shows are keeping people glued to their screens week after week. Whereas, movies get watched once, then forgotten, and not so many people want to spend their time to rewatch the movie the finished watching.\
**Recommendation**: Maintaining and adding more TV shows will be valuable to maximize ongoing subscriber retention, while movies can be the fuel to pull new subscribers who want to watch certain movies.\
